newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Redland hit by Germany, sterling woes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Redland hit by Germany, sterling woes.

text.p: Shares in British building materials group Redland slid after it warned that its German business was still suffering and that the strong pound was sapping its earnings.

Rudolf Agnew, Redland chairman, told a meeting of shareholders on Wednesday that fourth quarter sales in continental Europe were slightly below expectations and that continued margin pressure in Germany was hitting profits.
Another blow was news that sterling's recent strength against the mark was hitting foreign earnings.

This latest trading update, given at an extraordinary general meeting to approve restructuring of the European roofing business, dampened hopes of a turnaround in Germany -- Redland's biggest market accounting for 40 percent of sales.
Redland shares closed down 29 pence at 365 1/2p, with other German-dependent stocks skidding in its wake.
RMC, already weakened by a stock overhang, fell 20-1/2p to 973p, while BPB due to report on Thursday fell 11p to 348-1/2p and Pilkington 2p to 154p.
Analysts expressed their dismay and warned of possible profit forecast downgrades for Redland which they had hoped was on course for recovery in Germany.
"We had thought the German market was flat and there were some signs of a Redland recovery. So this latest news is a disappointment," said one analyst.
"If sterling continues this way, we'll be downgrading."

Michael Rubie, analyst at Credit Lyonnais Laing, said the German update was "a touch disappointing" and said that Sterling's impact would have to be worked into the figures leading to a "slight easing back" in his forecast.
Redland's half year results in September saw profits reel due to bad weather and weak markets in the first quarter.

But the chief executive Robert Napier heralded a turnaround, predicting better results for the second half, though full year figures were unlikely to recover fully. The latest news indicates there is no end in sight for the pain in Germany.
Another sector player, RMC Group, had been more cautious, with its chief executive Peter Young predicting that the German downturn would continue through 1997.
In recent days, building material stocks reliant on the German market have been depressed by the German economy's weakness and the pound's strength against the mark.

German jobless figures topped the four million level for the first time in October and the country's labour market has said that the economy is not growing sufficiently to curb unemployment growth in 1997.
Infrastructure spending also remained tight across Europe as governments in Germany and France reigned in budgets in a race to comply with the economic criteria for European Monetary Union in 1999.
